exercises.title: Nearby repair shops
exercises.prompt: Design repair-shop search for 20 million places and 5,000 searches/s, peaking at 15,000. Return at most 50 visible shops within 5 km. Ordinary updates may lag one minute; owner removal must apply immediately. Cover indexing, borders, updates, and hot areas.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Find visible places within 5 km. Define result limit, sorting, one-minute update lag, and an immediate owner-removal rule. Straight-line distance is sufficient.

### Size
Assume 20 million places and 5,000 searches/s, peak 15,000. At 300 candidates/search, peak filtering is 4.5 million candidates/s; benchmark density skew before sharding. State bytes per place and cache hit assumptions.

### Model
GET /places?lat=&lon=&radius=&cursor=. Place(id, point, details, visible, version) is authoritative. A spatial index and optional coarse-cell cache are derived. Use a stable tie-breaker for pagination.

### Flow
Cover the query circle, read candidate IDs, batch-fetch details, filter distance and visibility, then rank. Owner updates commit source plus change event together. Version-aware index consumers replay safely.

### Stress
Test a cell boundary, dense city, removed place still cached, and out-of-order index event. Immediate removal needs an authoritative deny/visibility check; the one-minute search freshness budget alone cannot satisfy it.

### Operate
Observe candidate count, hot cells, cache hit rate, latency, and update lag. Rebuild a versioned index alongside the old one, compare results, switch gradually, and retain rollback. Bound coordinate retention.

### Explain
A spatial database minimizes moving parts. A cell index supports independent serving scale but needs border coverage and replay. More precise cells reduce candidates while increasing fan-out and cache fragmentation.

exercises.title: Walking time replaces distance
exercises.prompt: Now return places reachable within ten minutes on foot. Explain what changes and why a circle is insufficient.
exercises.solution: A circle can generate initial candidates, but walking reachability needs a routable graph with crossings, access rules, and path costs. Use a conservative candidate region, then route/rank with travel-time costs. State approximation and compute budgets. Rivers and restricted roads make straight-line order wrong. Reuse the place source and versioned updates; monitor route-service latency separately.

exercises.title: A missing cafe
exercises.prompt: Bad design: hash the user coordinate, read only that exact cell, and return every place ID from it. Name two wrong results and repair the read path.
exercises.solution: A nearby cafe across the border is missed; a far corner in the same cell can be outside the requested radius. Cover every cell intersecting the query circle, then check true distance. Recheck current visibility. Test points exactly on boundaries and just inside/outside the radius.

questions.prompt: A shop is across the cell border but 10 m away. What must the query do?
options: Search intersecting cells, then filter distance.
Increase every cell to city size.
questions.explanation: Cell boundaries are index boundaries, not product distance rules.

questions.prompt: What should own a shop name?
questions.explanation: The index is a rebuildable view of stable place records.

questions.prompt: Which estimate exposes dense-area cost?
options: Only the number of API methods.
The length of a place name.
Candidates inspected per search at peak load.
questions.explanation: Candidate count multiplied by search rate estimates filtering work.

questions.prompt: A removed place remains in a cached candidate list. What enforces immediate removal?
options: A current authoritative visibility check or fast deny path.
questions.explanation: Freshness of a derived view alone cannot promise immediate removal.

modules.title: Track nearby friends safely
modules.outcome: Places rarely move. People move all the time. Separate the latest location from the list of people allowed to see it.

sections.title: Moving people change the problem

quick.title: Moving people change the problem
quick.explanation: Places rarely move. People move all the time. Separate the latest location from the list of people allowed to see it.
quick.example: A friend sends a new location every ten seconds. Last week’s position is not useful.
quick.tip: Location needs a timestamp and an expiry.

sections.content: Define distance, expected refresh interval, offline behavior, and visibility controls before choosing transport. Distinguish precise coordinates, approximate presence, and the claim that a friend is currently nearby. Their retention and freshness requirements differ.

sections.title: Route live updates

quick.title: Route live updates
quick.explanation: A connection server keeps a live link to the phone. A location service records a versioned update and tells interested watchers.
quick.example: A reconnect may land on a different server. The old connection must not own the new session.
quick.tip: A socket is a route, not the source of truth.

sections.content: WebSocket gateways maintain session routes. A location record carries user_id, session/version, point, received_at, and expiry. Server-issued sequence/session epochs can reject packets from obsolete sessions. Do not blindly trust phone clocks or allow one user to publish another user’s position.

sections.title: Limit who watches whom

quick.title: Limit who watches whom
quick.explanation: Use the friendship graph and nearby cells to limit updates. Subscribe only to relevant people or areas.
quick.example: Sending every movement to a million users creates huge fan-out.
quick.tip: Filter interest before sending updates.

sections.content: A pub/sub layer can route relevant updates to gateways with interested clients. Use friend relationships first and spatial grouping when needed. Subscription churn and hot areas are costs. Coarse cells narrow candidates; the final distance check decides actual proximity.

sections.title: Treat privacy as part of the flow

quick.title: Treat privacy as part of the flow
quick.explanation: Check permission when a watcher subscribes and when an update is sent. Old subscriptions must not keep working after permission is removed.
quick.example: A blocked friend should stop receiving location even if their socket stays connected.
quick.tip: Revoking access must reach live subscriptions.

sections.content: Authenticate the publisher and watcher. A permission version, subscription invalidation, or send-time check must enforce a stated revocation deadline. A database update followed by asynchronous cache expiry cannot silently claim instant revocation. Avoid retaining precise trails unless needed.

sections.title: Handle stale and late updates

quick.title: Handle stale and late updates
quick.explanation: Discard an older location version. Expire silent users. Label a location stale rather than pretending it is current.
quick.example: A delayed packet from before a train ride must not move the user backwards.
quick.tip: New arrival does not always mean new location.

sections.content: Choose behavior for disconnection and packet reordering. Expiry helps hide old presence but is not a guarantee of deletion from every derived store. Observe end-to-end update age, subscription fan-out, blocked-send failures, and gateway reconnect storms.

quick.tip: Promise → path → failure → repair.

examples.title: Follow a small worked example
examples.content:
### Contract
Show two friends approximately nearby. Updates refresh every ten seconds. Stop sharing within two seconds of blocking.
### Size
100,000 online users / 10 seconds = 10,000 inbound updates/s. Outbound load also depends on active watchers.
### Model
Location(user, session_epoch, sequence, point, expires_at) plus a separate permission record.
### Flow
Phone → authenticated gateway → version check → latest location → allowed watchers → their gateways.
### Stress
Predict: what if an old socket publishes after a reconnect?

Reject its obsolete session epoch. A new TCP connection alone does not invalidate old application messages.
### Operate
Track update age and revocation delay. Expire silent locations.
### Explain
WebSocket gives timely transport. It does not prove freshness, permission, or ordering by itself.

exercises.title: Friends at a festival
exercises.prompt: Design nearby friends for one million online users. Phones update every ten seconds. Show friends within 2 km; hide positions older than 30 seconds. Blocking must stop sharing within two seconds. Cover session changes, permission checks, and overloaded festival cells.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Nearby friends within 2 km; 10-second updates; stale locations hidden after 30 seconds; permission revocation effective within two seconds. Define approximate distance and offline behavior.

### Size
One million online users / 10 seconds = 100,000 updates/s before bursts. If each has five active watchers, roughly 500,000 outbound updates/s. Bound watchers and measure skew.

### Model
Location(user_id, session_epoch, sequence, point, received_at, expires_at); Friendship and SharingPolicy as authority. Gateway routing is ephemeral. Authenticate both sides and never trust client-supplied owner identity.

### Flow
Accept an authenticated location only if its session/version is current. Store latest state with expiry, find eligible nearby watchers, check permissions, publish to their gateways. Reconnect resubscribes from current allowed state.

### Stress
Test reordered updates, duplicate packets, old sessions, and a block during delivery. Invalidate subscriptions and enforce a send-time policy/version check within the two-second budget. Treat uncertain/expired data as unavailable.

### Operate
Measure update age, revocation delay, fan-out, active subscriptions, and reconnect rate. Rate-limit publishers and avoid location trails in logs. Rebuild routing after gateway loss without reviving expired locations.

### Explain
Per-user subscriptions are simple for small friend lists; area channels may reduce routing overhead in dense regions but need strict filtering. Precision and retention increase privacy cost.

exercises.title: Battery-saving mode
exercises.prompt: Phones may now update only once per minute. The UI still asks for nearby friends. What promise must change?
exercises.solution: Keep the server receipt time and display last-updated age. With one-minute sampling you cannot honestly promise a ten-second location. Use approximate/stale labels, a wider uncertainty region, or request an explicit refresh with user consent. Preserve revocation checks independently of location sampling. Explain the battery, precision, and freshness trade-off.

exercises.title: Old subscriptions leak
exercises.prompt: Bad design: permission is checked only when a WebSocket opens. Blocking updates the database but does not touch subscriptions. Repair it.
exercises.solution: Apply permission checks to subscriptions and deliveries. Publish a policy-version invalidation and remove live watchers; enforce the two-second deadline with a bounded refresh or authoritative send gate. Test an already connected blocked watcher and an event queued before the block. Hide old cached locations from newly unauthorized queries.

questions.prompt: Which record prevents a delayed old session from replacing a new location?
options: A current session epoch and sequence.
questions.explanation: Application versions reject obsolete sessions and older updates.

questions.prompt: Why is inbound update rate not the full capacity estimate?
options: Each update may fan out to many watchers.
questions.explanation: Outbound work is update rate multiplied by relevant active watchers.

questions.prompt: A phone last updated 90 seconds ago. What should the app do?
options: Hide or clearly mark it stale under the agreed contract.
Move it to the cell center.
questions.explanation: A last-known point does not establish a current location.

questions.prompt: What must a block operation affect?
options: Live delivery permission as well as stored friendship state.
questions.explanation: Already established subscriptions can otherwise keep leaking location.

modules.title: Build maps and route guidance
modules.outcome: A map image and a route answer solve different problems. Serve reusable map tiles through a CDN. Compute routes from a road graph.

sections.title: Separate maps from routes

quick.title: Separate maps from routes
quick.explanation: A map image and a route answer solve different problems. Serve reusable map tiles through a CDN. Compute routes from a road graph.
quick.example: Ten users can share the same map tile but need ten different routes.
quick.tip: Tiles are pictures. Routes are paths.

sections.content: Clarify map viewing, route search, and turn-by-turn navigation. A viewport requests tiles by zoom/x/y. Tile traffic is highly cacheable and bandwidth-heavy. Personalized route traffic depends on origin, destination, mode, restrictions, and current graph version.

sections.title: Model roads as a graph

quick.title: Model roads as a graph
quick.explanation: Junctions are points. Road segments connect them. Segment cost can include travel time, direction, and turn restrictions.
quick.example: The shortest line may cross a river with no bridge.
quick.tip: Distance alone is not a driving route.

sections.content: Route search uses directed edges, turn restrictions, and travel-time weights. Dijkstra/A* are starting points; large road graphs often need hierarchical preprocessing. State approximation and update trade-offs instead of promising a planet-wide graph scan per request.

sections.title: Version the map data

quick.title: Version the map data
quick.explanation: Build tiles and route graphs from a known map version. Publish new versions safely. Keep a rollback path.
quick.example: A closed road must not stay open in the graph after the map update.
quick.tip: Know which map version answered.

sections.content: An offline pipeline validates road changes and builds versioned graph partitions and tiles. Publish a manifest, canary route results, and retain the previous version. Graph seams and cross-region trips need connected boundary nodes.

sections.title: Add live traffic carefully

quick.title: Add live traffic carefully
quick.explanation: Traffic changes route costs. Keep base roads separate from recent traffic estimates. Label old traffic data.
quick.example: An old congestion sample should not overwrite a newer road-speed estimate.
quick.tip: Stable graph. Changing costs.

sections.content: Live probes need sampling, privacy controls, map matching, outlier handling, and freshness. Aggregate speeds by road segment and time window. A cost change may invalidate a cached route even when road geometry is unchanged.

sections.title: Keep navigation useful on failure

quick.title: Keep navigation useful on failure
quick.explanation: Cache the current route on the phone. Reroute when needed. Batch location telemetry and keep it private.
quick.example: Losing signal in a tunnel should not erase the next turn.
quick.tip: A route already delivered should survive a brief outage.

sections.content: Track tile hit rate, route latency, route failures, traffic age, reroute frequency, and version mismatch. If traffic ingestion fails, fall back to historical travel time with an honest indication. Do not make navigation depend on uploading each location synchronously.

examples.content:
### Contract
A campus shuttle app shows a map and routes along allowed roads. Live traffic is optional.
### Size
100 tiles per view × 100 views/s = 10,000 tile requests/s before caching. Route requests are a separate smaller workload.
### Model
Versioned tiles and directed road edges with travel-time costs.
### Flow

### Stress

No. Keep route geometry and turns locally; mark traffic updates unavailable.
### Operate
Watch failed routes and graph versions. Compare sample trips before switching graphs.
### Explain
Serving tiles cheaply does not solve route computation. Each path needs its own capacity and failure plan.

exercises.title: A country-wide driving app
exercises.prompt: Design map browsing and car routes. Expect 50,000 map views/minute, 40 tiles/view, and route searches from 10% of views. Target p 95 route latency under two seconds. Traffic may lag two minutes. Keep current directions usable during a network outage.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Support map browsing and car routes for one country. p 95 route latency target two seconds; traffic may lag two minutes. Keep last route available offline. Exclude transit schedules and street-view imagery.

### Size
At 50,000 map views/min and 40 tiles/view, about 33,333 tile requests/s before CDN hits. If 10% request a route, about 83 route requests/s. Peaks and reroute storms need separate headroom.

### Model
Tiles keyed by map_version/zoom/x/y. Road graph has directed segments, geometry, restrictions, and costs. Route API accepts origin, destination, mode, and avoid rules; returns versioned geometry and turns.

### Flow
Build and publish validated versioned graph/tiles. CDN serves tiles. Route service snaps endpoints to roads, searches with travel-time costs, and returns steps. Traffic ingestion updates recent costs. Client stores route for brief outages.

### Stress
Test disconnected graph components, a one-way road, closed bridge, stale traffic, and a regional graph boundary. Reroute conservatively; if traffic is stale, use historical costs and label the estimate.

### Operate
Observe route latency, no-route rate, tile cache hits, traffic age, and graph version. Canary known trips, compare distances/times, switch manifests gradually, and retain rollback. Minimize precise-location logs.

### Explain
A global graph is simpler conceptually but expensive to search and update. Hierarchical graphs speed long trips at preprocessing cost. Tiles use CDN capacity; routing uses compute. Do not size them as one workload.

exercises.title: A bridge closes now
exercises.prompt: A bridge closes immediately after graph version publication. How do you stop new routes using it without rebuilding all tiles?
exercises.solution: Apply a versioned road-closure overlay checked by route search and route-cache validation. Invalidate affected active routes and suggest rerouting. Tile imagery may update later; routing safety rules must use the newer closure data. Preserve expiry, authority, and rollback of overrides. Track closure-to-route enforcement delay.

exercises.title: One cache for everything
exercises.prompt: Bad design: cache every route for one day keyed only by origin and destination. Repair the key and invalidation rules.
exercises.solution: Include travel mode, avoid rules, graph version, and an appropriate origin/destination normalization. Traffic-aware routes need a bounded time bucket or dependency invalidation; emergency closures require a current closure check. Private user options must not leak through shared cache entries. A one-day TTL cannot honor two-minute traffic freshness.

questions.prompt: What is a map tile best served through?
options: A fresh shortest-path search per pixel.
A user-specific queue for each pixel.
A versioned object path and CDN.
questions.explanation: Tiles are reusable content; routing is a different request path.

questions.prompt: Why model roads as directed edges?
options: One-way roads and allowed travel directions matter.
Every road can always be used both ways.
Direction only changes the tile color.
It removes the need for costs.
questions.explanation: Road connectivity and direction constrain valid routes.

questions.prompt: Traffic ingestion stops. What is an honest fallback?
options: Claim every route has live traffic.
Historical costs with a stale-traffic indication.
Wait forever before returning any route.
questions.explanation: Base geometry can still support useful routes with weaker time estimates.

questions.prompt: What must an emergency closure affect first?
questions.explanation: Tiles can lag while route decisions enforce current closures.

modules.title: Build a durable message queue
modules.outcome: Define when a producer may believe a message is safe. Also define how long consumers can replay it.

sections.title: A queue owns a promise

quick.title: A queue owns a promise
quick.explanation: Define when a producer may believe a message is safe. Also define how long consumers can replay it.
quick.example: A message only in one machine’s memory can vanish after that machine fails.
quick.tip: Accepted must have a durability boundary.

sections.content: Choose retained pub/sub or a task queue explicitly. This module builds a retained partitioned log with independent consumer groups. A producer acknowledgment refers to the configured replicated commit boundary. A consumer acknowledgment means group progress, not that every external effect happened exactly once.

sections.title: Partition the log

quick.title: Partition the log
quick.explanation: A partition is an ordered list with numbered positions. Different partitions run in parallel. Order is local to each partition.
quick.example: All updates for one order use the same key. Two unrelated orders can use different partitions.
quick.tip: More partitions give parallelism, not global order.

sections.content: Append messages with partition offsets. The partition key keeps related events together. Consumer-group assignments grant one active owner per partition within that group; ownership epochs fence stale workers during rebalance. Changing partition count may change key placement and ordering, so plan migration.

sections.title: Replicate before the right reply

quick.title: Replicate before the right reply
quick.explanation: A leader accepts writes. Followers copy them. The reply rule and safe leader election together decide what survives a failure.
quick.example: A follower that missed acknowledged data must not become leader and silently lose it.
quick.tip: A safe reply needs a safe next leader.

sections.content: Replication, minimum eligible replicas, producer acknowledgment policy, and election eligibility are one design. Refuse unsafe writes/elections when the contract requires no acknowledged-message loss. Disks and replication do not prevent all losses: define the supported failure model and recovery point.

sections.title: Separate work from progress

quick.title: Separate work from progress
quick.explanation: A consumer offset says how far a group has processed. Saving it too early loses work. Saving it after work can cause repeats.
quick.example: A worker updates a database, crashes before saving its offset, then sees the same message again.
quick.tip: Replay-safe effects make retries useful.

sections.content: Commit the business effect and deduplication record in one local transaction where possible. Then advance the consumer position. A crash between them repeats delivery but the effect remains safe. Broker transactions have a scope; an arbitrary external email or payment service is not automatically included.

sections.title: Bound backlog and recover

quick.title: Bound backlog and recover
quick.explanation: Retention is finite. Watch the oldest unread message and consumer lag. A growing queue cannot fix a permanently slow worker.
quick.example: If arrivals are 300/s and workers handle 200/s, backlog grows 100/s.
quick.tip: A buffer buys time, not infinite capacity.

sections.content: Capacity includes ingress bytes, replicated bytes, retention storage, and consumer read traffic. Segment files support sequential I/O and retention deletion. Track per-partition lag age, disk headroom, replication health, and rebalance rate. Consumers behind retention need snapshot recovery or a documented data-loss response.

quick.title: Close the lesson. Tell the story.
quick.explanation: Use the recap picture to explain the design aloud. Then hide it and try again.
quick.example: What if a worker crashes after its effect?
quick.tip: Promise → path → failure → repair.

examples.content:
### Contract
Store order events for two days. Billing and analytics read independently. Keep order-local sequence.
### Size
1,000 messages/s × 1 KB × 172,800 s ≈ 173 GB raw. Three copies need about 518 GB before indexes and headroom.
### Model
Topic → partition → offset. Each consumer group has its own progress.
### Flow
Key by order ID → append → replicate to the commit rule → reply. Consumers process and then commit offsets.
### Stress
Predict: billing saves an invoice and crashes before the offset commit.

The message returns. A unique order/event identity prevents a second invoice in the same database transaction.
### Operate
Watch oldest unread age and disk space, not only message count.
### Explain
Partition order is enough for one order. Global order would restrict parallelism without helping this contract.

exercises.title: A seven-day event log
exercises.prompt: Design a retained message queue for 20,000 messages/s of 1 KB each. Keep seven days. Billing and analytics consume independently. Preserve order per order ID. Survive one replica failure without losing acknowledged messages. Explain consumer crash recovery and storage needs.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Retained pub/sub log, order-local ordering, independent consumer groups, seven-day replay, at-least-once delivery. No acknowledged-message loss for one replica failure under the chosen commit/election rules.

### Size
20,000 messages/s × 1 KB = 20 MB/s ingress. Seven days ≈12.1 TB raw decimal, about 36.3 TB at three copies before overhead. Include read fan-out, bursts, and headroom.

### Model
Topic metadata maps partitions to leaders/replicas and epochs. Message carries key, event_id, payload, checksum. Offset is partition-local. Group offsets and assignments are durable control metadata.

### Flow
Producer resolves leader, appends by key, waits for the supported replicated commit boundary, and retries with stable identity if uncertain. Consumer processes durably, records deduplication with local effect, then commits offset.

### Stress
Crash a leader before and after acknowledgment. Elect only a sufficiently caught-up replica. Fence old leaders/workers. A consumer crash after effect but before offset replays safely. A gap older than retention needs recovery rather than pretend replay.

### Operate
Measure lag age, disk headroom, replication lag, rejected writes, and rebalance duration. Rotate/delete segments under retention. Throttle tenants and test restore. Queue age and bytes need alerts.

### Explain
Partitions increase throughput but limit ordering scope. Waiting for safer replication raises latency and can reduce availability. A broker alone cannot make unrelated external effects exactly once.

exercises.title: A slow consumer misses retention
exercises.prompt: Analytics is offline for ten days, but retention is seven. Design recovery without claiming all events can still be replayed.
exercises.solution: Detect the offset falling behind the retained beginning. Stop normal consumption and recover from a trusted snapshot plus retained tail, or an archive if one was deliberately kept. State any unrecoverable gap. Version the snapshot and align it to partition positions. Raising retention now cannot recreate deleted events.

exercises.title: Offset committed too soon
exercises.prompt: Bad consumer: save offset; charge customer; if it crashes, restart from saved offset. Repair the order and the external effect boundary.
exercises.solution: Saving the offset first can skip a charge. Process with a durable operation identity, provider idempotency/status lookup, and local state transitions; commit the offset after durable handling. A crash can replay the message, so retries reuse the identity. Reconcile unknown provider results. Moving the offset line alone does not make the remote charge atomic.

questions.prompt: What order does a partitioned log naturally provide?
options: One universal order across all topics.
No need to choose a message key.
questions.explanation: Partition-local positions do not define an order between different partitions.

questions.prompt: A consumer crashes after saving its effect but before saving progress. What helps?
options: Replay with a durable deduplication identity tied to the effect.
questions.explanation: Delivery can repeat; the effect must handle that repeat.

questions.prompt: Arrivals are 300/s and service is 200/s. What happens?
questions.explanation: A buffer cannot repair sustained arrival rate above service capacity.

questions.prompt: What must accompany a strong producer acknowledgment?
options: Election rules that reject a successor missing committed data.
questions.explanation: A safe acknowledgment can still be undone by an unsafe leader election.

modules.title: Measure systems and send useful alerts
modules.outcome: Choose signals that show whether users can finish their task. Add machine signals to explain failures.

sections.title: Start from a user problem

quick.title: Start from a user problem
quick.explanation: Choose signals that show whether users can finish their task. Add machine signals to explain failures.
quick.example: CPU can be low while every checkout request fails.
quick.tip: Measure the symptom before the cause.

sections.content: Use latency, traffic, errors, and saturation to cover service symptoms and capacity. Define the objective and which request population counts. An alert should point to a useful action; dashboards can carry lower-urgency information.

sections.title: A metric is a series

quick.title: A metric is a series
quick.explanation: A metric name plus labels identifies a time series. Every new label combination adds storage and work.
quick.example: region=west is bounded. user_id can create millions of series.
quick.tip: Labels multiply.

sections.content: A series is identified by metric name and complete label set. 100 services ×20 instances ×5 status classes already gives 10,000 possible series. Unbounded request IDs or user IDs can explode memory/index size. Logs/traces are often better for individual-request detail.

sections.title: Collect and store in stages

quick.title: Collect and store in stages
quick.explanation: Collectors buffer samples. Ingestion validates them. A time-series store serves time-range queries and rollups.
quick.example: A short collector outage should not block the application request.
quick.tip: Monitoring must not become the outage.

sections.content: Choose push or pull from deployment and discovery needs. Buffer with a bounded disk queue and a deliberate drop policy. Validate types, timestamps, and allowed labels. Write recent data at fine resolution, then roll up older windows while retaining enough detail for the actual questions.

sections.title: Alerts need state

quick.title: Alerts need state
quick.explanation: Evaluate a rule over time. Group related failures and remember when an alert opens or resolves.
quick.example: One noisy service should not send a thousand separate pages.
quick.tip: Detect → group → notify → resolve.

sections.content: Rule evaluation needs pending/firing/resolved states, a duration threshold, grouping, deduplication, and delivery retries. An alert fingerprint makes retry-safe notifications possible. Alert delivery failure needs its own visible signal. Keep routing and on-call configuration auditable.

sections.title: Test the monitor itself

quick.title: Test the monitor itself
quick.explanation: Missing samples can mean the collector died. Track data freshness and test the notification path too.
quick.example: A quiet dashboard may be healthy or disconnected.
quick.tip: No data is a state, not automatically success.

sections.content: Check ingestion lag, missing targets, evaluation delay, and notification success. Redundant monitoring or an external probe catches failure of the main monitoring stack. Avoid using raw private user data in labels. Bound query cost and isolate expensive users.

sections.title: Retell the whole design

quick.title: Close the lesson. Tell the story.
quick.explanation: Use the recap picture to explain the design aloud. Then hide it and try again.
quick.example: What if the collector stops sending data?
quick.tip: Promise → path → failure → repair.

examples.title: Follow a small worked example
examples.content:
### Contract
Alert when checkout error rate stays above 5% for five minutes. Only page if enough requests occurred.
### Size
100 instances ×10 metrics × one sample/10 seconds =100 samples/s before label combinations.
### Model
Series(name, labels) and timestamped samples. Alert state is separate durable state.
### Flow
Collect → ingest → query a five-minute window → pending/firing rule → grouped notification.
### Stress
Predict: zero samples arrive. Is error rate zero?

No. Evaluate missing-data health separately. A denominator of zero does not prove success.
### Operate
Test a synthetic failing request and confirm that someone receives the alert.
### Explain
Store request IDs in traces, not as unbounded metric labels.

exercises.title: A checkout monitoring platform
exercises.prompt: Design monitoring for 10,000 instances with 100 series each, sampled every ten seconds. Dashboards should be under 30 seconds old. Alert on sustained checkout errors for five minutes, with a traffic floor. Include cardinality limits, missing data, and notification failure.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Collect service latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Dashboard freshness under 30 seconds. Page after a sustained five-minute checkout error condition with a traffic floor; handle missing data separately.

### Size
10,000 instances ×100 series each /10-second interval =100,000 samples/s. At 16 bytes raw/sample, one day is about 138 GB before labels/indexes/replication. Cardinality is a separate capacity dimension.

### Model
Series identified by name and allowed labels; samples by timestamp. AlertRule and AlertState store thresholds, duration, fingerprint, destinations, and last notification. Separate samples from alert delivery state.

### Flow
Collectors buffer bounded samples; ingestion validates labels/timestamps; time-series storage accepts writes; evaluators read windows; sustained conditions create grouped alert state; notification workers retry safely.

### Stress
Test collector outage, partial scrape failure, duplicate sample, expensive query, and notification timeout. Missing data triggers a distinct health rule. Preserve alert state across evaluator failover to avoid duplicate pages.

### Operate
Watch ingestion age, missing targets, query p 95, evaluator delay, and notification delivery. Downsample older data under an explicit retention policy. Add an external probe and regularly test paging.

### Explain
Pull simplifies target health visibility; push suits some short-lived or constrained jobs. Rich labels improve debugging but grow series count. Long windows reduce noise but delay detection.

exercises.title: Every request adds a new label
exercises.prompt: A team adds request_id to a latency metric. Explain the damage and give another way to debug one request.
exercises.solution: Each distinct request ID creates a separate series, multiplying index/storage costs and weakening aggregation. Remove the unbounded label, keep bounded service/region/status dimensions, and use traces or logs for request-level detail. Link a sampled trace from an aggregate metric if supported. Add ingestion label/cardinality budgets.

exercises.title: A misleading quiet dashboard
exercises.prompt: Bad rule: if no samples exist, display zero errors and resolve every alert. Repair it.
exercises.solution: Represent missing/stale data explicitly. Evaluate target availability and ingestion freshness separately from service error rate. A service rule needs a valid denominator and sufficient traffic; missing telemetry must not erase a still-unresolved incident. Test a collector outage while the application is failing.

questions.prompt: Which label is most likely to cause unbounded series growth?
questions.explanation: The number of unique label combinations determines series cardinality.

questions.prompt: No samples arrive. Which conclusion is valid?
options: Telemetry freshness is unknown or unhealthy.
questions.explanation: No data and a measured zero are different states.

questions.prompt: Why keep pending/firing alert state?
options: To guarantee every error pages immediately.
To require a sustained condition and control repeated notifications.
questions.explanation: State lets the rule distinguish a transient spike from a sustained incident.

questions.prompt: What verifies the full monitoring path?
options: A synthetic failure that reaches an observed notification.
questions.explanation: Collection, evaluation, routing, and delivery must all work.

modules.title: Count events without counting twice
modules.outcome: Raw events let you rebuild a total. Aggregates make reads cheap. Give each event a stable identity.

sections.title: Keep raw facts and useful totals

quick.title: Keep raw facts and useful totals
quick.explanation: Raw events let you rebuild a total. Aggregates make reads cheap. Give each event a stable identity.
quick.example: A retry of the same click must not become a new click.
quick.tip: One fact. One identity.

sections.content: Define counted event, deduplication scope, dimensions, and correction policy. Retain raw events under a privacy and cost budget. Separate operational dashboards from billing-quality finalized totals. A stable event_id must represent the same logical event across retries.

sections.title: Choose the clock

quick.title: Choose the clock
quick.explanation: Event time says when the click happened. Processing time says when the server handled it. Delays make them different.
quick.example: A phone offline for two minutes uploads an older click now.
quick.tip: Arrival time is not event time.

sections.content: Window by event time if the product asks when the action happened. Client time needs sanity bounds or trusted attribution. Processing-time windows are simpler but move delayed actions into later buckets. State which promise you choose rather than mixing them.

sections.title: Define late data rules

quick.title: Define late data rules
quick.explanation: A window groups events by time. Decide how long to wait for late events and whether published totals can be corrected.
quick.example: A 12:00 click arriving at 12:03 may update an earlier minute.
quick.tip: A final total needs a lateness policy.

sections.content: A watermark is a progress estimate used to decide which windows are ready; it does not prove no older event will ever arrive. Allow bounded late updates and version corrected outputs, or route overly late events to a correction path. Explain what users see during changes.

sections.title: Make replay safe

quick.title: Make replay safe
quick.explanation: Save processing state and output consistently, or use versioned/upserted results. Restarting from a checkpoint must not add the same partial total twice.
quick.example: Writing +100 twice after a crash doubles the result.
quick.tip: Replaying a batch must replace or deduplicate its effect.

sections.content: Checkpoint source positions and aggregation state together under the chosen engine semantics. Write output with a stable window/key/version identity or a transaction. Dedup state needs retention covering the supported replay horizon. Exactly-once totals require agreement among source, state, and sink.

sections.title: Handle hot keys and backfills

quick.title: Handle hot keys and backfills
quick.explanation: A popular ad can overload one worker. Split partial counts, then combine them. Keep rebuild output separate until validated.

exercises.title: Live ad-click totals
exercises.prompt: Design counts for 100,000 click events/s of 200 bytes each, grouped by ad/country/minute. Dashboard lag under ten seconds. Late events may correct totals for five minutes. Handle duplicate delivery, hot ads, restart, and a backfill without double counting.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Count ad clicks by ad, country, and minute. Dashboard updates within ten seconds. Accept late data for five minutes; later arrivals go to correction processing. Deduplicate stable event IDs.

### Size
100,000 events/s ×200 bytes =20 MB/s, about 1.73 TB raw/day before replication. Estimate dedup-state size from replay horizon and IDs/s, not only result-row count.

### Model
Click(event_id, ad_id, event_time, country); source partition/offset; result keyed by ad/country/minute plus revision. Keep raw input and processing checkpoints; define ID scope and retention.

### Flow
Ingest durable events, validate timestamp bounds, deduplicate, assign event-time windows, combine partial counts, and publish versioned results. Track progress per partition and document late correction behavior.

### Stress
Replay a checkpoint, duplicate one click, delay a partition, and overload a hot ad. A watermark cannot guarantee no late event. Use stable output identities and consistent checkpoints; split hot keys and combine without repeating partial contributions.

### Operate
Observe lag, duplicates, late arrivals, state size, and totals versus raw sampled recomputation. Backfill to a separate version; validate and switch readers atomically. Keep auditable corrections without retaining unnecessary personal fields.

### Explain
Faster provisional counts trade certainty for freshness. Longer lateness windows need more state and delay finality. Global dedup forever is expensive; state the supported horizon.

exercises.title: A billing team needs finalized totals
exercises.prompt: Live dashboards accept revisions. Billing now needs reproducible finalized totals. What extra boundary and evidence are needed?
exercises.solution: Publish a versioned finalized dataset after a stated lateness cutoff and correction policy. Preserve input ranges/checkpoints, aggregation version, dedup rules, and reconciliation evidence. Later corrections create a new auditable adjustment/version instead of silently changing an issued result. Avoid claiming the watermark proves all possible events arrived.

exercises.title: A backfill doubles totals
exercises.prompt: Bad rebuild: replay all raw events and increment the same live counter again. Repair the rebuild procedure.
exercises.solution: Write recomputed results into a new version keyed by aggregation dimensions and window. Deduplicate according to stable event identity and replay horizon. Compare totals, samples, and input coverage, then switch the reader manifest. Retain rollback. Do not merge a complete replacement dataset as additional increments.

modules.title: Reserve inventory without overselling
modules.outcome: A search result may be a little old. A confirmed booking must reserve real inventory.

sections.title: Search is a hint. Booking is a promise.

quick.title: Search is a hint. Booking is a promise.
quick.explanation: A search result may be a little old. A confirmed booking must reserve real inventory.
quick.example: Two people can both see one room left. Only one may book it.
quick.tip: Recheck at the write boundary.

sections.content: Define whether inventory is per room or room type, whether overbooking is allowed, and how payment relates to confirmation. This exercise forbids overselling. Search can use cached availability, but the authoritative booking transaction must recheck all nights.

sections.title: Model every night

quick.title: Model every night
quick.explanation: Hotels usually sell a room type for a date range. Check each night, not just one availability flag.
quick.example: A Friday-to-Sunday stay uses Friday and Saturday night inventory.
quick.tip: One stay. Several inventory rows.

sections.content: Inventory(hotel_id, room_type, date, capacity, held, confirmed, version) supports a date-range stay. Reservation(id, user, dates, status, hold_expiry, request_key) records intent. A single is_available boolean cannot represent availability across arbitrary date ranges.

sections.title: Make one atomic decision

quick.title: Make one atomic decision
quick.explanation: Check and reserve all required nights in one transaction. Use locks or conditional versions so two requests cannot both win.
quick.example: Reading available=1, then writing 0 later allows two winners.
quick.tip: Check and change together.

sections.content: Lock inventory rows in a stable date order, or use conditional versioned updates with retry of the whole transaction. Ensure every night has capacity before committing any decrement. A failed night rolls back the whole reservation. Unique request keys handle client retries.

sections.title: Separate holds and payment

quick.title: Separate holds and payment
quick.explanation: A short hold can protect inventory during payment. Give it an expiry and explicit state. A timeout is not proof payment failed.
quick.example: A successful payment can arrive after the hold expires. The system needs a policy for that case.
quick.tip: Every pending state needs an exit.

sections.content: Keep held, confirmed, expired, canceled, and payment_unknown transitions explicit. Releasing a hold and accepting a payment success must race through a conditional state transition. A late success may require a refund if inventory can no longer be reserved; never silently overbook.

sections.title: Retry safely and reconcile

quick.title: Retry safely and reconcile
quick.explanation: Use a stable booking request ID. Repeating the request should return its existing result, not reserve another room.
quick.example: The client lost the reply but the booking was committed.
quick.tip: Retry the identity. Do not create a new booking.

sections.content: Observe booking conflicts, hold age, abandoned inventory, payment unknowns, and oversell checks. Reconcile provider outcomes with local state. A cache must not decide correctness. Test overlapping date ranges and expiry versus success, not only two identical requests.

examples.content:
### Contract
Sell one remaining room for Friday night. No overbooking. Payment can be delayed.
### Size
The dangerous load is simultaneous bookings for the same room type and night, even when total traffic is small.
### Model
Inventory(date, capacity, held, confirmed) and Reservation(request_key, state, expiry).
### Flow
Lock the inventory row → verify capacity → create hold and request identity → commit. Pay using the same operation identity.
### Stress
Predict: two buyers read one remaining room before either writes.

A separate read then write oversells. One atomic guarded transaction lets only one reserve it.
### Operate
Expire abandoned holds through a state transition. Reconcile late payment success.
### Explain
Cached search helps speed. Authoritative inventory decides the booking.

exercises.title: Rooms across several nights
exercises.prompt: Design hotel room-type booking:100,000 searches/s and 1,000 booking attempts/s. Search may lag 30 seconds. Never oversell any night. Hold rooms for five minutes during payment. Cover multi-night transactions, retries, expiry, and a late payment success.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Reserve room types for check-in inclusive/check-out exclusive dates. No overselling. Search may lag 30 seconds; booking is authoritative. Hold inventory for five minutes during payment and define late-success behavior.

### Size
100,000 searches/s and 1,000 booking attempts/s are different paths. A popular hotel/date can concentrate conflicts. Estimate rows per stay and transaction duration; partition by hotel while keeping a stay transaction local.

### Model
Inventory(hotel, type, night, capacity, held, confirmed, version); Reservation(id, owner, dates, state, expires_at, request_key); PaymentAttempt with stable provider key. Unique request identity and authorized ownership checks.

### Flow
In one transaction lock all nights in stable order, verify capacity, create a hold and request result, update inventory, and commit. Payment proceeds outside the database lock. Conditional transitions convert the live hold to confirmed or release it.

### Stress
Test two buyers for the last room, one unavailable middle night, duplicate requests, and payment success racing expiry. Roll back all nights on failure. A late success after release needs explicit re-reservation/refund policy, not forced confirmation.

### Operate
Monitor conflicts, hold expiry lag, stale search age, unknown payment outcomes, and inventory consistency. Use an outbox for confirmations. Reconcile payment state. Test recovery of an expiry worker after an outage.

### Explain
Pessimistic locks simplify contention reasoning but can wait/deadlock; stable lock order helps. Optimistic versions work under lower contention but need whole-transaction retry. A cache lock alone is not the authoritative inventory rule.

exercises.title: An assigned seat instead
exercises.prompt: The business now sells exact seats for a show, not pooled room types. What changes in keys, holds, and concurrency?
exercises.solution: Use show_id/seat_id as the inventory identity and a conditional transition from available to held with owner/expiry/version. A unique active seat allocation prevents double sale. A multi-seat booking needs an all-or-nothing policy or explicit partial acceptance. Payment, expiry races, request deduplication, and late-success handling still apply. The date-range capacity loop becomes exact-seat state transitions.

exercises.title: Two winners for one room
exercises.prompt: Bad code: if read_available(night)>0: create_booking(); decrement(night). Repair it for a three-night stay.
exercises.solution: Begin one transaction, lock all three inventory rows in deterministic order, verify each available capacity, then update every row and insert the unique-request reservation. Commit once. If any night fails, roll back all changes. Alternatively use versioned conditional updates with whole-transaction conflict retry. Prove correctness with two concurrent overlapping stays.

questions.prompt: A three-night stay has no capacity on night two. What should happen?
options: The whole reservation transaction fails without partial inventory loss.
Reserve nights one and three silently.
questions.explanation: The booking promise spans every required night.

questions.prompt: What protects a retried request after a lost response?
options: A random booking ID on each retry.
A unique durable request identity and stored outcome.
questions.explanation: The retry must find the original operation rather than allocate again.

questions.prompt: Payment succeeds after a hold was released. What is required?
options: An explicit conditional recovery or refund policy.
Call the timeout a failure forever.
questions.explanation: The payment result and inventory state must be reconciled honestly.

modules.title: Deliver and search email
modules.outcome: Sending email has several states. A server may accept a message while the recipient server has not accepted it yet.

sections.title: Submission is not inbox delivery

quick.title: Submission is not inbox delivery
quick.explanation: Sending email has several states. A server may accept a message while the recipient server has not accepted it yet.
quick.example: The recipient server is down. The outgoing message stays queued for retry.
quick.tip: Accepted here does not mean delivered there.

sections.content: Distinguish client submission, durable local acceptance, remote SMTP acceptance, recipient mailbox placement, and read state. Protocol acceptance cannot prove a human saw the mail. Specify temporary/permanent failure handling and a visible delivery status model.

sections.title: Separate content and mailbox state

quick.title: Separate content and mailbox state
quick.explanation: Keep large bodies and attachments in blob storage. Keep mailbox ownership, folders, flags, and message IDs in indexed records.
quick.example: Marking a message read should not rewrite its 50 MB attachment.
quick.tip: Bytes and mailbox state have different jobs.

sections.content: Store immutable body/attachment blobs with size and integrity metadata. MailboxEntry(user_id, message_id, folder, flags, version) provides user-scoped queries and synchronization. Deduplication of shared blobs is separate from authorization of every mailbox reference.

sections.title: Build retry-safe delivery

quick.title: Build retry-safe delivery
quick.explanation: An outbound queue retries temporary failures. Keep a stable internal identity and delivery attempts. Stop on permanent failure or policy expiry.
quick.example: A connection drops after the remote server accepts the mail but before its reply arrives.
quick.tip: An uncertain remote outcome can still duplicate mail.

sections.content: Commit outgoing intent before returning accepted. Workers lease attempts, obey per-domain limits, retry temporary errors with backoff, and create a bounce/failure record for permanent errors. A remote timeout may be unknown. Internal deduplication cannot force every SMTP recipient to deduplicate.

sections.title: Search is a private derived view

quick.title: Search is a private derived view
quick.explanation: Build a search index from stored mail. Check mailbox ownership again when returning results. Deletes must reach both views.
quick.example: A stale search index must not show a message from another user’s mailbox.
quick.tip: Search helps find. Ownership allows access.

sections.content: An outbox/change stream feeds the mailbox search index. Version-aware events avoid restoring deleted mail. Check current mailbox membership and deletion policy on result hydration. Define index freshness and removal deadlines; do not make search the source of truth.

sections.title: Abuse and recovery are core paths

quick.title: Abuse and recovery are core paths
quick.explanation: Limit sending, inspect unsafe attachments, protect credentials, and recover queued work after a crash.
quick.example: One compromised account should not exhaust every sender’s quota.
quick.tip: Protect the recipient and the shared service.

sections.content: Inbound boundaries validate size and identity policy, scan attachments under a quarantine state, and enforce abuse budgets. Observe delivery age, domain failures, spam complaints, search lag, and storage integrity. Keep private message content out of routine logs; audit authorized access.

### Size

exercises.title: A team email service
exercises.prompt: Design email submission, inbox listing, read flags, attachments, and private search for two million messages/day at 100 KB average. Search may lag 30 seconds. Explain durable acceptance, remote retries, uncertain delivery, deletion, and abuse limits.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Provide client submission, mailbox listing, read flags, attachment download, and private search. Local accepted means durable content plus delivery intent. Remote acceptance/read are separate states; search may lag 30 seconds.

### Size
Two million messages/day at 100 KB average =200 GB/day raw before attachments and replication. Size peak SMTP connections, mailbox reads, and search independently. Large attachments dominate tail storage and bandwidth.

### Model
Message(id, body_ref, attachment_refs, integrity); MailboxEntry(user, message, folder, flags, version); Delivery(id, destination, state, attempts, next_try). Stable internal send key deduplicates client retries.

### Flow
Validate sender and size, persist content and local mailbox/delivery intent durably, then return accepted. Delivery workers use per-domain concurrency and retries. Change events feed search. Result hydration rechecks user mailbox ownership.

### Stress
Test lost submit response, remote acceptance with lost reply, duplicate inbound mail, stale search deletion, and worker restart. Preserve uncertain remote outcomes; do not promise unique external delivery without recipient cooperation.

### Operate
Observe queue age, domain rejection, bounce rate, search lag, blob integrity, and abuse quotas. Quarantine suspicious attachments, protect credentials, and audit access without copying message bodies into logs.

### Explain
An external search engine speeds development but adds synchronization and privacy boundaries. A custom index adds maintenance cost. Blob content and small mutable mailbox records should evolve independently.

exercises.title: Urgent mailbox deletion
exercises.prompt: A user deletes a message and it must disappear from search immediately, even though indexing takes 30 seconds. How?
exercises.solution: Commit a tombstone/current mailbox visibility change in the authoritative mailbox store. Search may still return the stale ID, but hydration filters it against current access/deletion state. Purge index entries asynchronously and apply the stated blob retention/legal policy separately. Test stale index pages and direct attachment URLs with expiring scoped access.

exercises.title: Remote timeout means resend forever
exercises.prompt: Bad worker: any timeout creates a new message ID and retries immediately forever. Repair identity, retry policy, and status.
exercises.solution: Reuse the original logical send identity and keep a durable delivery-attempt record. A timeout is unknown; retry under bounded time/attempt policy with backoff and domain limits. Record remote references where available. Distinguish permanent rejection from transient failure. Internal identity prevents duplicate local work, but arbitrary SMTP recipients may still see duplicate delivery.

questions.prompt: What protects private search results?

questions.explanation: A stale derived index must not grant current access.

questions.prompt: Can an internal message ID guarantee exactly-once SMTP delivery?

No; the remote effect needs cooperation or a weaker promise.

modules.title: Store objects and keep them intact
modules.outcome: Metadata maps a bucket and key to a committed object version. Storage nodes hold the bytes.

sections.title: Separate names from bytes

quick.title: Separate names from bytes
quick.explanation: Metadata maps a bucket and key to a committed object version. Storage nodes hold the bytes.
quick.example: Renaming a pointer should not move every byte through the API server.
quick.tip: Metadata finds. Data nodes carry.

sections.content: Object APIs operate on bucket/key/version identities. Metadata stores ownership, placement, size, checksum, and commit state. Data nodes serve large byte streams directly under scoped authorization. A metadata cache must not expose private or deleted content.

sections.title: Commit after the bytes are safe

quick.title: Commit after the bytes are safe
quick.explanation: Upload parts to storage, check integrity, then publish a complete object version. Incomplete uploads must not appear as valid objects.
quick.example: A broken upload has four of five parts. Readers should not receive a partial file as complete.
quick.tip: Upload → verify → publish.

sections.content: Multipart uploads have an upload identity and part identities/checksums. Completion verifies the expected parts and commits one visible version conditionally. Concurrent overwrites need a defined version/order policy. Acknowledgment is tied to the durability contract, not merely receipt by a gateway.

sections.title: Copies and coding have costs

quick.title: Copies and coding have costs
quick.explanation: Replication keeps full copies. Erasure coding keeps data and repair pieces. Coding can save space but makes reads and repair more complex.
quick.example: Three copies of 100 TB use about 300 TB before overhead.
quick.tip: Space saved can become repair work.

sections.content: With k data and m parity pieces, ideal space expansion is(k+m)/k, but fault tolerance requires pieces across independent failure domains. Coding does not remove metadata or repair needs. Durability probability and availability depend on failure correlation, detection, repair bandwidth, and enough remaining readable pieces.

sections.title: Listing is its own access pattern

quick.title: Listing is its own access pattern
quick.explanation: Looking up one object by key and listing keys by prefix need different index support. Hashing names evenly does not make sorted listing cheap.
quick.example: photo/2026/ may span many metadata shards.
quick.tip: Spread writes. Plan ordered reads.

sections.content: Hash(bucket,key) balances direct metadata lookup but prefix listings need an ordered secondary index or scatter/gather with a cursor contract. Define snapshot/listing consistency under concurrent writes. Avoid promising filesystem hierarchy or atomic folder rename from slash characters alone.

sections.title: Repair and garbage collection

quick.title: Repair and garbage collection
quick.explanation: Check stored pieces for corruption and rebuild missing ones. Delete unreferenced uploads only after proving no committed object still needs them.
quick.example: A slow upload must not lose parts because a cleanup worker guessed it was abandoned.
quick.tip: Deletion needs ownership, state, and a grace rule.

sections.content: Scrubbing detects silent corruption using checksums. Repairs are scheduled with bandwidth/capacity limits. Garbage collection uses committed references, upload expiry/state, and grace periods; retain versions/tombstones as required. Observe repair backlog, missing pieces, integrity failures, and metadata/data mismatch.

### Size

### Model

### Operate

### Explain
Cheap space is not the only target. Repair speed and failure domains matter.

exercises.prompt: Design private object storage with GET/PUT/DELETE and prefix LIST. Store 1 PB logical data with objects up to 5 GB. Publish only complete uploads. Compare replication and 6+3 coding. Explain metadata, checksums, failure domains, orphan cleanup, and repair.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
GET/PUT/DELETE and prefix LIST for private objects, up to 5 GB each. A successful completed PUT exposes one complete version. Specify overwrite/list consistency and supported node/rack failures.

### Size
Assume 1 PB logical data: three replicas need 3 PB before overhead. A6+3 erasure code has 1.5x ideal expansion. Compare repair traffic and spare capacity; include multipart remnants and older versions.

### Model
Bucket ownership; Object(bucket,key,version,state,size,checksum,placement); Upload(id,parts,expiry); storage-piece records across failure domains. Ordered listing index is separate from balanced direct lookup.

### Flow
Authenticate, allocate upload, send parts to data nodes, verify integrity and required durable placement, then atomically publish the committed version. Reads resolve current authorized metadata and stream verified pieces.

### Stress
Fail upload midway, lose completion reply, corrupt a piece, lose a rack, and race overwrite/delete. Retry completion by upload ID. Do not expose incomplete bytes. Verify coding pieces lie in distinct failure domains and repair before redundancy is exhausted.

### Operate
Observe incomplete uploads, repair backlog/age, checksum failures, free capacity, and metadata mismatch. Rate-limit repair against serving capacity. Garbage-collect only safely unreferenced/expired data with a grace protocol. Test restore, not only replication.

### Explain
Replication is simpler and fast for small/hot objects; erasure coding reduces expansion for larger/cold objects but costs CPU and repair bandwidth. Prefix listing requires planned indexes; hashing alone does not provide it.

exercises.title: A rack disappears
exercises.prompt: A6+3 coded object has all nine pieces on one rack. Explain why the code does not protect against a rack loss and repair the placement policy.
exercises.solution: A code survives loss of at most three pieces only if enough independent pieces remain. Losing the rack loses all nine. Spread pieces across independent rack/zone failure domains under an explicit policy, reserve repair capacity, monitor placement violations, and test loss of the largest supported domain. Durability is not just the number of parity pieces.

exercises.title: Partial upload becomes visible
exercises.prompt: Bad code: create visible object metadata, upload parts, then return success. A worker may crash mid-upload. Repair publication and cleanup.
exercises.solution: Use an uploading state separate from visible committed versions. Upload and verify all parts, satisfy the declared durability boundary, then publish the complete version with a conditional transaction. Keep completion idempotent by upload ID. Garbage-collect abandoned parts by expired upload state and reference checks; never delete parts referenced by a committed version.

questions.prompt: When should a complete object become visible?
options: As soon as the first part arrives.
After required bytes are verified and the committed version is published.
Whenever a gateway allocates an ID.
questions.explanation: Visibility is a commit decision, not proof that upload started.

questions.prompt: What is ideal expansion for 6+3 erasure coding?
questions.explanation: (6+3)/6=1.5, before metadata and operational overhead.

questions.prompt: Does hash-based key lookup solve prefix listing?
options: Yes, automatically sorted on every shard.
No; ordered listing needs its own index or scatter/gather plan.
questions.explanation: Balanced direct lookup and sorted range access are different patterns.

questions.prompt: What makes garbage collection safe?
options: Lifecycle/reference checks and a defined grace rule.
Deleting every part older than one minute.
questions.explanation: A slow or retried upload can still legitimately need its parts.

modules.title: Rank players with clear rules
modules.outcome: Decide whether scores are totals, best scores, or latest scores. Specify ties and the season boundary.

sections.title: Define what rank means

quick.title: Define what rank means
quick.explanation: Decide whether scores are totals, best scores, or latest scores. Specify ties and the season boundary.
quick.example: Two players have 100 points. The product must say whether they share a rank.
quick.tip: A ranking needs a comparison rule.

sections.content: Define rank convention: competition rank(1,1,3), dense rank(1,1,2), or a unique order with a deterministic tie-breaker. Different sorted-set APIs may return positions rather than the desired shared rank. State freshness and whether exact global rank is required.

sections.title: Use an ordered score index

quick.title: Use an ordered score index
quick.explanation: A sorted set can support score changes, top players, and player rank. Keep player identity as a stable member.
quick.example: A hash table finds a score quickly but does not directly give everyone’s order.
quick.tip: Point lookup and ordered lookup differ.

sections.content: For moderate scale, a sorted set per season supports ordered queries while a durable score source provides recovery. Store player details separately and hydrate only returned IDs. Score precision and tie-break encoding need care; do not lose integer accuracy in a packed floating-point score.

sections.title: Trust validated game results

quick.title: Trust validated game results
quick.explanation: Clients should not freely write their own final score. Apply each validated match result once.
quick.example: A retry of a 10-point match must not add another 10 points.
quick.tip: Validate once. Apply once per result ID.

sections.content: Validate results server-side. A stable match/result ID and unique applied-event record prevent repeated increments. Commit deduplication and durable score change together, then update the derived sorted index through replay-safe events. A cache command alone does not make the whole workflow durable.

sections.title: Split carefully

quick.title: Split carefully
quick.explanation: A single ordered index is easy until it is too large or hot. Shards can produce local top lists, but exact global rank needs more work.
quick.example: A player is rank 10 on one shard. That does not tell their worldwide rank.
quick.tip: Local rank is not global rank.

sections.content: Top-K merges can be efficient: ask each shard for its local top-K, then merge. Exact rank of an arbitrary player needs the number of players ahead across all shards under a consistent snapshot/freshness contract. A simple local-rank lookup cannot answer it.

sections.title: Rebuild without mixing seasons

quick.title: Rebuild without mixing seasons
quick.explanation: Keep score events or authoritative totals so the serving index can be rebuilt. Key every result by season.
quick.example: A delayed result from last season must not change this season’s board.
quick.tip: Season is part of the identity.

sections.content: Use season_id in input, totals, and ordered-index keys. Rebuild a new index from a trusted checkpoint plus tail, validate top/rank samples, then switch. Track score-to-index lag, replay duplicates, memory, hot players, and rank-query latency.

### Contract

### Size

### Model

exercises.title: A weekly game leaderboard
exercises.prompt: Design a board for ten million players and 20,000 score events/s. Return top 100 and each player’s position within two seconds of a validated result. Define ties, retry safety, season rollover, rebuild, and the limits of sharding.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Weekly leaderboard, valid match points, exact top 100, player position, deterministic ties, and two-second score freshness. Define whether position or shared rank is required; exclude client-authoritative scores.

### Size
Ten million players and 20,000 score events/s. Estimate real sorted-index overhead and replication memory, not only raw score bytes. Benchmark one board before sharding; arbitrary-rank queries add read cost.

### Model
Result(event_id, season, player, validated_delta); authoritative totals and applied-event IDs; season-scoped ordered projection. Tie ordering includes an explicit stable secondary field. Player profile is separate.

### Flow
Validate trusted match result, commit deduplication plus score total, publish replay-safe projection update, then serve top 100/rank with bounded freshness. Include the projection version/age where useful.

### Stress
Test repeated result, out-of-order projection update, season rollover, and index loss. Apply total versions rather than stale additive cache updates. Exact global position after sharding needs counts ahead across shards with a consistency contract.

### Operate
Observe index lag, duplicate IDs, memory/headroom, hot players, and query p 95. Rebuild next to live index from checkpoint plus tail; validate and switch. Reject results for the wrong season.

### Explain
One sorted index is simple but has memory/write limits. Sharded top-K merging is tractable; exact arbitrary rank costs cross-shard work. Weaker approximate rank may be a product option, never an unstated substitution.

exercises.title: Only top 100 is needed
exercises.prompt: Remove arbitrary-player rank from the requirements. How does the sharded serving path become simpler?
exercises.solution: Each shard returns its local top 100 under the same season and tie ordering. Merge those lists to choose the global top 100. A player outside their shard top 100 cannot enter the global top 100 because at least 100 players in that shard already precede them. State snapshot/freshness limits; this does not solve exact arbitrary global rank.

exercises.title: Duplicate score increments
exercises.prompt: Bad handler: receive match result; increment sorted-set score; acknowledge. A timeout causes the same result to be sent again. Repair it.
exercises.solution: Persist a stable validated result ID and atomically apply it with the authoritative total exactly once within that transaction. Publish a versioned total update to the serving index; consumers ignore older versions/repeated updates. A separate dedup write after the increment leaves a crash gap. Rebuild the index from durable totals if lost.

questions.prompt: Why define tie rules before picking a rank API?
options: All products use the same tie rule.
Position and shared-rank conventions can produce different answers.
questions.explanation: A sorted position is not automatically the product’s requested rank.

questions.prompt: What makes score retries safe?
options: A new random ID on every retry.
A stable validated result ID tied atomically to the durable score change.
questions.explanation: The result identity must share the transaction with its effect.

questions.prompt: Can local rank 10 identify global rank?
options: No; other shards may contain players ahead.
Only if the name is unique.
questions.explanation: Global rank requires information about the rest of the population.

questions.prompt: What prevents old-season events affecting a new season?
options: Season identity on input, totals, and serving keys.
questions.explanation: The boundary must be part of the data model and validation.

modules.title: Handle payments and uncertain outcomes
modules.outcome: Track requested, pending, succeeded, failed, and unknown outcomes. A network timeout says the reply is missing, not that no money moved.

sections.title: A payment is a state machine

quick.title: A payment is a state machine
quick.explanation: Track requested, pending, succeeded, failed, and unknown outcomes. A network timeout says the reply is missing, not that no money moved.
quick.example: The provider charged successfully just before the connection broke.
quick.tip: Timeout means unknown.

sections.content: This is architecture practice, not a live payment integration. Separate authorization, capture, refund, and settlement according to product scope. Unknown is a durable state with a recovery action. Never infer provider failure merely from a missing response.

sections.title: One intention needs one identity

quick.title: One intention needs one identity
quick.explanation: Reuse a stable idempotency key for the same payment intent. Check that the amount and currency stay the same.
quick.example: Clicking Pay twice must not create two independent charges.
quick.tip: Same intent. Same key. Same parameters.

sections.content: An idempotency record binds tenant/intent/key to request fingerprint and result. Unique creation and state transitions prevent local races. Provider keys have documented scope and retention; retain local operation identity and provider references beyond a single HTTP request.

sections.title: Keep provider state and local records aligned

quick.title: Keep provider state and local records aligned
quick.explanation: Record the intent before calling the provider. Save its reference. Handle callbacks and status queries as repeatable state updates.
quick.example: The callback may arrive before the original API reply.
quick.tip: Every path meets the same state transition.

sections.content: Persist intent, execute the provider call without holding a long database lock, then record a conditional outcome. Authenticate and deduplicate webhooks; validate provider references and allowed transition order. Status queries and reconciliation repair missed callbacks. A late failure must not overwrite a confirmed success.

sections.title: Record money with an audit trail

quick.title: Record money with an audit trail
quick.explanation: A payment status is not a ledger. Ledger entries explain what moved and why. Reconcile them with provider records.
quick.example: A succeeded flag cannot explain a later refund or settlement difference.
quick.tip: Status tells where. Entries tell how much.

sections.content: Use append-only balanced ledger entries under a defined currency and accounting boundary; corrections are new entries. Compare internal payments, ledger effects, and provider settlement/report data. Surface discrepancies for investigation rather than auto-inventing a matching state.

sections.title: Retry without hiding uncertainty

quick.title: Retry without hiding uncertainty
quick.explanation: Retry transient failures under the provider’s documented key scope and expiry. Reconcile unknown or mismatched results.
quick.example: A new key after each timeout can create a second charge.
quick.tip: Find the first outcome before creating another intent.

sections.content: Use tokens rather than storing raw sensitive card data in this exercise. Enforce amount/currency ownership, least privilege, audit access, and safe logging. Observe unknown-outcome age, duplicate intent attempts, callback lag, reconciliation differences, and refund backlog.

### Contract
Pay 100 units once for one order. The provider supports idempotency and status lookup. A lost reply remains pending/unknown.
### Size

### Model
PaymentIntent(id, order, amount, currency, state, provider_key, provider_ref).

### Stress
Predict: the provider succeeds, the reply is lost, and the user retries.

Find the existing intent. Reuse the same provider key or query its status. Do not create a fresh charge key.
### Operate
Reconcile aged unknown states and settlement records. Keep secrets out of logs.
### Explain
Idempotency reduces repeated effects within its scope. Reconciliation handles remaining uncertainty.
