exercises.title: A retry-safe checkout payment
exercises.prompt: Design payments peaking at 2,000 requests/s against a provider quota of 1,500/s. A payment may succeed even if its reply is lost. The provider has idempotency keys with finite retention and a status API. Cover intent identity, callbacks, ledger linkage, refunds, and reconciliation.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
One payment intent per order amount/currency revision. Distinguish pending, success, terminal failure, and unknown. Provider supports a bounded idempotency contract and status lookup. Refunds are separate linked operations.

### Size
2,000 payment requests/s peak, provider quota 1,500/s. Admission/queueing must bound excess 500/s and expiry; a growing queue is not extra quota. Size status-query and reconciliation traffic too.

### Model
PaymentIntent(id, owner, order, amount_minor, currency, fingerprint, state, provider_key/ref, version); webhook dedup record; ledger operation link; reconciliation record. Use integer minor units with currency rules.

### Flow
Atomically create/find intent by stable scoped request key, verify fingerprint, and persist pending. Call provider with the same key. Conditional transitions unify replies, signed callbacks, and status checks. Commit local success plus downstream outbox atomically.

### Stress
Test lost response after provider success, concurrent retry, duplicate/out-of-order callback, and key retention expiry. Keep unknown durable. Never retry under a new provider key while the original result may have succeeded; query/reconcile or escalate.

### Operate
Observe unknown age, duplicate intent conflicts, provider errors/quota, callback lag, and settlement differences. Protect tokens, validate webhook signatures, restrict refunds, and keep audit records. Do not log raw payment credentials.

### Explain
Provider idempotency helps but has scope/expiry and does not reconcile every bookkeeping discrepancy. Local transactions, repeatable remote identity, and reconciliation solve different failure boundaries.

exercises.title: The key has expired
exercises.prompt: A payment is still unknown after the provider’s idempotency retention ends. Why is a new charge request unsafe, and what should happen?
exercises.solution: A new or expired key may no longer deduplicate the original successful effect. Query using the saved provider reference and reconcile against provider reports; keep the intent blocked from a fresh automatic charge while uncertain. Escalate unresolved cases under an explicit operational policy. Local record retention and provider idempotency retention are different boundaries.

exercises.title: Timeout becomes failure
exercises.prompt: Bad code: on timeout mark payment failed; retry with random UUID. Show a double-charge timeline and repair it.
exercises.solution: Timeline: provider captures chargeA; response is lost; local code marks failed; retry creates chargeB. Repair with a durable stable payment intent/key, explicit unknown state, status query or same-key retry within provider scope, and conditional callback handling. Reconciliation confirms the final state. Never assume timeout proves no external effect.

questions.prompt: The charge request times out. What is known?
options: A new key is always safe.
questions.explanation: Missing response does not reveal whether the remote side committed.

questions.prompt: What must an idempotency key be bound to?
options: The same scoped intent and request parameters.
A new random key per retry.
questions.explanation: Reusing a key for changed parameters must be rejected or treated as a new explicit intent.

questions.prompt: Why still reconcile when a provider supports idempotency?
options: Internal state and provider/settlement records can still disagree.
Ledger entries are optional for every product.
questions.explanation: Remote identity reduces one failure class; missed updates and accounting differences remain.

questions.prompt: A late callback conflicts with a terminal success. What helps?
options: Validated conditional state transitions and deduplication.
questions.explanation: Arrival order alone is not a safe payment state machine.

modules.title: Move wallet money without losing the trail
modules.outcome: A transfer must debit one account and credit another by the same amount in one currency. Reject spending unavailable funds.

sections.title: Name the rule money must obey

quick.title: Name the rule money must obey
quick.explanation: A transfer must debit one account and credit another by the same amount in one currency. Reject spending unavailable funds.
quick.example: Sending 30 from a 100-unit wallet leaves 70 and adds 30 to the receiver.
quick.tip: No money created. No money lost.

sections.content: Define available balance, holds, currency, transfer limits, and whether negative balances are allowed. This exercise forbids them. Fixed minor-unit amounts avoid ordinary binary floating-point errors; currency precision and conversion need explicit rules.

sections.title: Use a ledger and a balance view

quick.title: Use a ledger and a balance view
quick.explanation: Append entries that explain every change. A balance is a useful view, but it must agree with the ledger.
quick.example: A refund is a new linked entry. Do not erase the old transfer.
quick.tip: Correct with a new entry.

sections.content: A double-entry journal balances signed amounts within the defined currency/transaction boundary. Entry identity, account, transfer ID, and correction links provide auditability. Maintain a materialized balance for fast admission, but verify it against the journal and protect it with the same transaction.

sections.title: Make the local transfer atomic

quick.title: Make the local transfer atomic
quick.explanation: When accounts share a database boundary, lock or version both balances and commit the entries together.
quick.example: Debiting the sender and crashing before crediting the receiver loses money in the visible state.
quick.tip: Two sides. One commit boundary.

sections.content: For a single database, lock both accounts in deterministic order, find/create the unique transfer request, verify available funds, write both entries and balances, then commit. Serializable/version-based alternatives require explicit conflict handling. A separate dedup insert after moving funds leaves a crash gap.

sections.title: Cross-shard transfers need a protocol

quick.title: Cross-shard transfers need a protocol
quick.explanation: Separate databases cannot share a simple local transaction. Choose an explicit coordination or reserve/commit workflow.
quick.example: Two independent writes with retries do not prove an atomic transfer.
quick.tip: A queue is transport, not an atomic commit.

sections.content: For separate shards, explain 2PC with coordinator recovery and possible blocking, or a durable reservation/state-machine protocol with pending states and compensation semantics. A saga is not automatically an atomic transfer visible to everyone. Define what each user can observe during recovery.

sections.title: Replay must rebuild the same state

quick.title: Replay must rebuild the same state
quick.explanation: Event replay works only when the rules are deterministic and versioned. Fence old leaders and validate snapshots.
quick.example: A replay rule that asks for today’s exchange rate changes yesterday’s outcome.
quick.tip: Same events. Same rules. Same state.

sections.content: Event-sourced processing needs an ordered durable command/event history, deterministic validation, fenced leadership, and snapshot positions. Consensus replicates a chosen history but does not make arbitrary external calls deterministic. Observe imbalance checks, held-funds age, rejected overdrafts, and recovery time.

examples.content:
### Contract
Transfer 30 units between two wallets in one database. No negative available balance. A retry returns the original result.
### Size
The contention risk is many transfers touching one account. Total users alone does not size that critical section.
### Model

### Flow

### Stress

The guarded transaction lets one succeed and rejects the other. Two stale balance reads would incorrectly approve both.
### Operate
Reconcile journal sums and materialized balances. Retry after a lost reply using the same request ID.
### Explain
This local transaction is a valid starting boundary. Sharding changes the correctness protocol, not just the connection string.

exercises.title: A same-currency wallet
exercises.prompt: Design wallet transfers at 5,000 transfers/s. No negative available balance. Retried requests must not move funds twice. Keep an audit trail. Start with a local transaction, then explain what changes when sender and receiver live on different shards.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Transfer within one currency, forbid negative available balances, keep auditable balanced entries, and deduplicate retries. Start with one transactional database; explicitly discuss the cross-shard extension.

### Size
5,000 transfers/s, at least two account touches and two journal entries per transfer. Hot merchant accounts may serialize far more work than average users. Benchmark transaction contention and journal growth.

### Model
Account(id, currency, balance, held, version); Transfer(id, scoped_request_key, from, to, amount, state); JournalEntry(transfer, account, signed_minor_amount). Unique request and balanced-entry checks inside the commit boundary.

### Flow
Validate ownership, currency, and amount. Lock accounts in stable order; find or create the request; verify funds; write both entries and balance updates; commit; return stored result. Publish downstream notifications through a local outbox.

### Stress
Race two spends, lose the response after commit, and crash between proposed debit/credit steps. One transaction prevents partial visibility. With separate shards choose a documented protocol; independent retrying writes cannot claim atomicity.

### Operate
Reconcile ledger entries with balance views, detect aged holds/pending transfers, monitor contention, and test restore/replay. Corrections append linked entries. Restrict privileged adjustments and avoid sensitive logs.

### Explain
A local transaction keeps the proof short. Sharding increases coordination and recovery work. Event sourcing enables replay only with deterministic versioned rules and correct replicated history; it is not a substitute for those guarantees.

exercises.title: A replay uses today’s rules
exercises.prompt: A recovery process replays transfers using the latest fee rate and current exchange rate. Why can balances change, and how should replay work?
exercises.solution: Historical effects must be reproducible. Store the already-decided fee/conversion amounts and rule version in committed events, or replay under the exact deterministic historical rules. External rates and wall-clock calls cannot silently affect old events. Snapshot state must identify the log position and code/data version; verify rebuilt totals against journal checks.

exercises.title: Debit now, credit later
exercises.prompt: Bad workflow: debit sender; publish queue event; consumer credits receiver. The database commit can succeed while publishing fails. Can this promise an atomic transfer? Repair the claim and design.
exercises.solution: It cannot claim atomic debit/credit across that gap. If accounts share a database, commit both with the journal and unique request in one transaction. If separated, use a durable coordinated protocol with reservations/pending states and recovery; an outbox preserves transfer intent but still does not make both databases one atomic boundary. State visibility and compensation limits.

questions.prompt: Two 70-unit transfers race against 100 available. What prevents both succeeding?
options: A shared guarded transaction or equivalent serializable admission rule.
questions.explanation: The funds check and debit need a concurrency boundary.

questions.prompt: How should an incorrect posted transfer be corrected?
questions.explanation: A preserved history explains both the original action and its correction.

questions.prompt: Does an outbox make two separate account databases atomic?
options: Yes if the event is small.
No; it preserves intent but needs a transfer protocol.
Only when a CDN is added.
questions.explanation: Reliable publication and atomic multi-database state are separate problems.

questions.prompt: What is needed for deterministic replay?
options: Current exchange rates for all past events.
A random seed chosen on every run.
Committed historical facts and versioned rules without fresh external decisions.
questions.explanation: Replay must reconstruct the original effects rather than decide new ones.

quick.title: Specify the matching rule
quick.explanation: An order book groups buy and sell orders by price. This exercise uses price first, then accepted order sequence.
quick.example: Two equal-price orders cannot both be first. Use the exchange sequence, not phone time.
quick.tip: Price first. Accepted sequence next.

sections.content: This is a simplified engineering exercise, not a trading system specification. Clarify limit orders, partial fills, cancel behavior, risk checks, and price-time priority. User/device timestamps are not a fair authoritative ordering source. A cancel racing a fill resolves by the accepted sequence.

sections.title: Keep one authority per book

quick.title: Keep one authority per book
quick.explanation: A single ordered owner for one symbol makes matching easier to reason about. Many symbols can use different owners.
quick.example: Two machines independently matching the same book may sell the same resting order twice.
quick.tip: One book. One fenced authority.

sections.content: A per-symbol book maintains price levels and FIFO queues at each price. Partitioning by symbol preserves a simple serial order. One very hot symbol remains a capacity limit; spreading it across independent matchers changes the matching protocol and fairness proof.

sections.title: Record before promising

quick.title: Record before promising
quick.explanation: Persist and replicate the accepted command sequence before the promised acknowledgment. Derive trades deterministically.
quick.example: An in-memory match lost on failover cannot support a durable success promise.
quick.tip: Fast is useful only with an honest durability rule.

sections.content: Durable admission, replicated log positions, deterministic matching, and trade IDs create a recoverable path. Risk reservations must prevent overcommit before acceptance. A success acknowledgment must identify whether it means received, durably accepted, or matched; those are different milestones.

sections.title: Keep market data separate

quick.title: Keep market data separate
quick.explanation: Order acceptance and matching are the critical path. Public price updates can use a replayable feed with sequence numbers.
quick.example: A viewer missing one feed packet should detect a gap and recover.
quick.tip: Trading state and viewing state differ.

sections.content: A market-data publisher emits sequenced snapshots/deltas from committed state. Clients detect missing sequence ranges and obtain a snapshot plus tail. Backpressure or feed drops must not stop the matching loop. A book viewer may be stale while trading admission remains available under its own limits.

sections.title: Recover without two active leaders

quick.title: Recover without two active leaders
quick.explanation: A standby replays the same committed commands. Failover fences the old owner and resumes from the correct position.
quick.example: A partitioned old leader must not keep publishing valid trades.
quick.tip: Failover needs fencing, not just detection.

sections.content: Standby recovery needs exact log position, deterministic code/data version, and leader epochs that downstream consumers enforce. Do not let two authorities produce valid effects. Measure durable-accept latency, match latency, queue age, feed gaps, and recovery time. Test cancel/fill races and failover after commit but before reply.

examples.content:
### Contract
One symbol accepts limit orders and cancellations. Price-time priority uses a server sequence. Accepted means durable, not immediately filled.
### Size
Measure the busiest symbol’s commands/s and latency. A thousand quiet symbols do not reveal one hot book’s limit.
### Model
Order(id, client_key, side, price_ticks, quantity, sequence, remaining). Price levels hold FIFO orders.
### Flow
Validate risk → assign sequence → commit replicated command → match deterministically → publish sequenced results.
### Stress
Predict: a cancel and a fill race.

Resolve by the accepted command sequence. A client timestamp cannot retroactively cancel an earlier committed fill.
### Operate
Standby replays committed history. Fence the old owner before accepting new authority.
### Explain
One serial book gives a clear ordering proof. Public feed delivery can scale separately.

exercises.title: A simplified order-matching service
exercises.prompt: Design limit orders and cancellations for 100 symbols at 100,000 commands/s. One symbol gets 60% of traffic. Use price-time priority. Explain durable acceptance, partial fills, cancel races, duplicate requests, market-data recovery, and fenced failover.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Limit orders, partial fills, and cancellations for 100 symbols. Price-time priority uses server accepted sequence. Durable acceptance is distinct from execution. Exclude complex order types and cross-venue routing.

### Size
100,000 commands/s total with 60% on one symbol. The hot book receives 60,000/s, so average 1,000/s per symbol is misleading. Benchmark durable append and matching separately with tail latency.

### Model
Order(client_key, symbol, side, price_ticks, quantity, remaining, sequence); price-level FIFO queues; durable commands and trade IDs; reserved funds/positions; leader epoch. Use bounded integer ticks/units.

### Flow
Authenticate and check limits, assign authoritative book sequence, durably replicate command under the acknowledgment contract, apply deterministic matching/cancel rules, record outputs, then publish executions and market-data deltas.

### Stress
Race cancel/fill, duplicate a client command, crash after commit before reply, and partition the old leader. Replay committed commands once by stable identities. Fence stale authorities in storage/output paths. A cancel cannot erase an earlier fill.

### Operate
Track durable-accept and match latency separately, hot-book queue age, feed gaps, standby lag, and recovery time. Rebuild from snapshot plus exact log tail; test state hashes. Apply backpressure/admission rather than silently dropping accepted orders.

### Explain
Per-symbol serialization is simple and parallel across symbols. A hot symbol remains a bound. Batching can improve throughput but adds latency. Replication improves recoverability only when commit/election/fencing rules preserve one accepted history.

exercises.title: A viewer misses feed messages
exercises.prompt: A market-data client sees sequence 100 followed by 105. How should it recover without affecting order matching?
exercises.solution: Detect the gap, stop claiming the local view is current, and request missing deltas if retained. Otherwise obtain a consistent snapshot at sequenceS plus all deltas afterS, buffering during synchronization. Use a separate replay/snapshot path with quotas so slow viewers cannot block matching. Execution and market-data delivery have different promises.

exercises.title: Two active matchers
exercises.prompt: Bad failover: after missing three heartbeats, start a new matcher; the old one may still send trades. Repair the authority rule.
exercises.solution: Use a coordinated leadership epoch/lease with enforced fencing in durable writes and effect publication. New authority resumes only from the committed sequence; downstream paths reject stale epochs. Heartbeat suspicion alone does not revoke an old process’s ability to write. Test a partition that isolates old/new leaders while both can reach some clients.

exercises.title: Nearby events with scarce seats
exercises.prompt: Without notes, design nearby event discovery plus exact-seat checkout.5,000 searches/s;500 hold attempts/s with 20x hot-show spikes. Search may lag 30 seconds. Never sell a seat twice. Holds last five minutes. A payment may succeed after a lost reply. Explain the seven phases and trace the hardest race.
exercises.solution:
### Contract
Find events nearby and sell exact seats. Search may lag 30 seconds; no double sale; payments can be unknown. Define ownership, hold expiry, and what accepted/paid/confirmed each mean.

### Size
Assume 5,000 searches/s,500 hold attempts/s, and a 20x hot-show spike. Size hot-seat contention, provider quota, and spatial candidates separately. Estimate which path reaches a limit first.

### Model
Event/place spatial view; authoritative ShowSeat(show,seat,state,owner,expiry,version); Reservation(request_key,state); PaymentIntent; outbox. Search and seat authority are separate views.

### Flow
Search cells then exact-filter event distance. Hold seats conditionally with request identity. Persist payment intent; call provider with stable key. Transition hold to confirmed only under valid state; publish notifications via outbox.

### Stress
Race two buyers, expire a hold during payment, lose a provider reply, and return a stale search result. Use current authoritative checks, unknown payment state, reconciliation, and an explicit refund/re-reservation policy.

### Operate
Monitor hold conflicts/age, provider unknown age, search lag, queue age, and confirmation correctness. Run a bounded hot-show load test, canary admission changes, and define rollback thresholds.

### Explain
Explain one rejected alternative for each important decision: cache-only locking, new payment keys on retry, and global message order. State why each fails or adds cost under the contract.

exercises.title: Rebuild a usage dashboard
exercises.prompt: In a later session, design per-tenant API usage totals from 100,000 events/s. Live totals may be revised for ten minutes. A monthly export must be reproducible. Handle duplicate delivery, one hot tenant, missing data, and a historical rebuild.
exercises.solution: Define stable event identity, trusted event time, lateness/correction boundaries, and tenant authorization. Keep raw retained facts and consistent checkpoints; publish versioned tenant/window results. Split hot keys into deduplicated partials. Finalize a versioned export with input ranges and rule versions. Backfill separately, compare, then switch. Monitor lag, missing partitions, duplicate rate, and reconciliation gaps. A watermark is not proof that every possible event arrived.

exercises.title: Review an unsafe failover
exercises.prompt: Architecture review: one leader updates wallet balances in memory, replies success, then sends events to a replica. After a heartbeat timeout a second leader starts. Both may write. List the broken promises and propose a minimal safe redesign.
exercises.solution: Success before durable replication can lose acknowledged transfers. Memory alone lacks a recoverable committed history. Heartbeat suspicion does not fence the old writer. Two authorities can overspend or fork balances. Start with a transactional durable ledger and protected balance updates plus stable request IDs; use an explicitly replicated commit/election protocol if failover is required. Fence stale epochs. Reconcile and test commit-before-reply, partition, and replay scenarios.

materials.protocol:
# Use one learning loop across both volumes

Volume 1 has 72 planned hours; Volume 2 adds 64. At 7 hours/week the full track is about 20 weeks, including review time within your weekly budget. This is a planning estimate, not a mastery guarantee. The original 12-week outline below applies to Volume 1 only.

Start with a short lesson and diagram. Study an example, then solve a new prompt before opening its reference. Request AI feedback, compare, repair one gap, and return after a delay. Try the visual labs to test races, retries, overload, and search borders.

# Learning protocol

## Why the activities are structured this way

Practice testing and distributed practice have broad support in learning research. The course therefore asks you to retrieve mechanisms without notes and revisit them after delays.

A good-looking notebook is an artifact of study, not proof of retrieval. [Dunlosky et al.](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/journals/pspi/learning-techniques.html).

Worked examples, self-explanation, and fading steps are useful when moving from studying solutions to independent problem solving. We use a fully annotated example, then fewer prompts, then a blank-page problem.

Guidance should decrease as skill grows. [Atkinson, Renkl, and Merrill](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ678596).

Retrieval can improve meaningful learning as well as factual recall; that motivates explanation and inference questions, not only flashcards.

The underlying experiments do not establish that this particular HLD course is optimal or guarantee interview performance. [Karpicke and Blunt](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21252317/).

## Before, during, and after an attempt

Before opening a solution, write your prediction: the dominant risk, the invariant, and the likely architectural decision. During the attempt, say the reason for each component aloud.

After feedback, identify a counterexample your original design mishandled. Repair that mechanism and later solve a changed problem without opening the repaired answer.

For a worked example, cover the next paragraph and predict the next decision. Ask: why does this step follow from the requirement?

What would make it unnecessary? Copying the diagram does not count.

In a partially guided exercise, fill missing reasoning before looking at the answer. In a final exercise, do not use the framework sheet until the timer ends.

## Recall queue

Schedule approximately +1, +3, +7, +14, +30, and +60 days from an attempt. These are convenient defaults, not uniquely optimal intervals.

Keep the weekly review budget to one hour: six short retrieval blocks, or three 20-minute blocks. Review failures and high-impact decisions first.

Later reviews can substitute for new material when gaps accumulate.

- +1: explain the main flow in five minutes.
- +3: answer one failure question in five minutes.
- +7: redraw in ten minutes, including durable acknowledgment.
- +14: compare with a different system in ten minutes.
- +30: solve a changed-constraint mini-design in ten minutes.
- +60: use the mechanism in a mixed mock.

Mark each as **retrieved**, **partly retrieved**, or **needed reference**, with the actual missing mechanism. When you fail, attempt first, inspect only the gap, then retry tomorrow.

When recall is easy, extend the gap or make the scenario less familiar. Mix older problem families only after you have initially learned their mechanisms.

## Decision cards

Keep about 20–30 high-value cards, not a transcript of the course.

Each card asks a decision question and records constraint → choice → alternative → cost → failure → condition that changes the choice.

Examples: “A sender timed out after the message might have persisted: how do we avoid duplicates?” and “A celebrity dominates one key: why does adding shards not automatically fix it?”

Use confidence predictions before attempts, then compare with observed performance. Feeling familiar while reading is not the same as producing the reasoning without help.

A correct multiple-choice selection with no explanation or elimination of alternatives is provisional.

## If you get stuck or fall behind

Use the smallest counterexample: two concurrent requests, one crashed worker, one unavailable replica, one hot key. Trace state before/after each step.

Ask for one narrow hint and label the attempt assisted. Repair the mechanism, then reattempt after a delay.

Keep three active gaps. Reduce new reading before removing retrieval.

Never restart the whole book because one mechanism is rusty. If your schedule changes, record the change and move the checkpoint honestly; do not convert “read” into “mastered.”
materials.rubric:
# Assessment rubric

Score eight dimensions 0–3 each, total 24: requirements; scale; data/interfaces; end-to-end flows; correctness/consistency; failure/operations/security; trade-offs/evolution; communication/adaptation.

For every dimension: 0 = missing or fundamentally wrong; 1 = terminology or partial reasoning requiring substantial help; 2 = a workable, justified mechanism without prompting; 3 = also handles a counterexample or changed constraint.

Attach concrete evidence from the attempt. Reasonable alternatives are acceptable when assumptions and consequences are explicit.

An unaided module gate needs **18/24**, every dimension at least 2, and no broken central invariant.

Do not award passing status merely for MCQs, matching the book, number of boxes, or an app-generated score. Early baseline scores identify gaps rather than pass/fail.

A correctness guarantee stronger than the proposed mechanism can deliver is a critical defect even if the diagram looks plausible.

For a module, complete P1, P2, the repair when supplied, and the checkpoint. Explain at least three of four checkpoint answers including why a tempting distractor fails.

Then complete a delayed altered-constraint explanation seven or more days later. An assisted attempt can complete practice but cannot establish independence.

If a local module gate uses a focused mini-design, mark irrelevant rubric dimensions unassessed and use a later full mock to establish the overall standard; do not invent scores for absent evidence.

For the foundation checkpoint, retrieve the framework without notes, redesign an anchor, and attempt an unfamiliar read-heavy or admission-control system. Record the achieved level: practice completed, foundation demonstrated, or independent transfer demonstrated.

For course graduation, submit three unfamiliar 45-minute designs from different families, one changed requirement per round, and one real-system architecture review.

At least two rounds must pass 18/24 with all dimensions at least 2; the remaining round receives a focused repair and later reattempt.

The real review must distinguish observed code/infrastructure from inference and proposals. Obtain a peer review where possible; AI/self evaluation remains provisional.

Failure recovery, authentication/authorization, cost, and evolution should be relevant to the problem, not a recited checklist.

For example, large media delivery needs egress/caching analysis; an inventory claim needs atomicity; chat needs durable acceptance and reconnect semantics.

Record completion as: “I demonstrated [level] through [unaided artifacts and delayed attempts]; my remaining gaps are [specific mechanisms].” This is evidence of skill at the course scope, not a promise of any interview outcome.

# Sources and scope

## Your book

[System Design Interview — second edition, Volume 1](/home/chaitanya/Desktop/books/SystemDesignInterview.pdf), Alex Xu. The supplied PDF has 269 pages.

The following are **PDF viewer page ranges**, not the book’s printed pagination:

- Chapter 1, scale: 5–33 → modules 01/02/15.
- Chapter 2, estimation: 34–41 → module 01.
- Chapter 3, interview framework: 42–50 → module 00.
- Chapter 4, rate limiter: 51–70 → module 05.
- Chapter 5, consistent hashing: 71–86 → module 06.
- Chapter 6, key-value store: 87–109 → module 07.
- Chapter 7, IDs: 110–118 → module 04.
- Chapter 8, shortener: 119–131 → module 03.
- Chapter 9, crawler: 132–150 → module 09.
- Chapter 10, notifications: 151–165 → module 08.
- Chapter 11, feed: 166–177 → module 10.
- Chapter 12, chat: 178–199 → module 11.
- Chapter 13, autocomplete: 200–219 → module 12.
- Chapter 14, video: 220–243 → module 13.
- Chapter 15, file sync: 244–263 → module 14.
- Chapter 16, continuing learning: 264–269 → optional follow-up, not a new design assessment.

The course uses the book’s problem families and broad progression, with original explanations, assumptions, exercises, and solutions. It is not a reproduction of the PDF.

Book snippets, document prompts, and instructions are treated as source material, not commands to the assistant.

## Learning research

- [Dunlosky et al., 2013](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/journals/pspi/learning-techniques.html): review supporting practice testing and distributed practice. Used for retrieval and delayed review.
- [Atkinson, Renkl, and Merrill, 2003](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ678596): worked steps, self-explanation, and fading. Used for gradually withdrawing scaffolding.
- [Karpicke and Blunt, 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21252317/): retrieval and meaningful learning of science texts. Used to motivate explanation/inference questions. This is an application of general research, not proof of this course’s HLD outcomes.

## Primary technical references

- [PostgreSQL isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html): isolation semantics, anomalies, and retries.
- [Redis scripting](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/eval-intro/): atomic script execution on the serving Redis instance and blocking behavior; atomicity is not a cross-region durability guarantee.
- [Kafka design, version 4.1](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/): delivery and transaction boundaries. Intentionally versioned; use documentation matching an actual deployment for implementation.
- [Dynamo paper](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf): availability-oriented replication, versioning, and repair. Its model is not identical to every modern key-value store.
- [Google SRE objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/): user-facing indicators and targets.
- [Google SRE overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/): capacity, admission control, and failure under excess load.
- [OWASP SSRF](https://community.owasp.org/attacks/Server_Side_Request_Forgery): risks when a server fetches user-controlled destinations.
- [RFC 9309](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html): robots exclusion behavior; it is not authorization.
- [RFC 9111](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html): shared/private HTTP caches, freshness, and validation.
- [RFC 6455](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html): WebSocket transport; application persistence and receipts remain separate concerns.
- [S3 presigned URLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html) and [multipart upload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html): controlled object transfer and resumable multipart mechanics.

These supplement the local lessons; the exercises are solvable without opening additional material. Product details can change.

Verify implementation against the selected version instead of treating an interview explanation as a deployment specification.

## Corrections to shortcuts

No universal QPS threshold forces SQL → NoSQL. Cache RAM depends on objects/locality/overhead, not daily bytes read.

Quorum overlap alone is not a complete linearizability protocol. Wall-clock sortable IDs do not prove causal order.

A WebSocket does not make delivery durable. A queue does not remove a sustained capacity deficit.

Replication does not replace tested backups. Cache invalidation does not automatically guarantee freshness.

Use each claim with an explicit contract and failure model.

## Volume 2 extension
Alex Xu and Sahn Lam, System Design Interview: An Insider’s Guide, Volume 2.
The supplied scanned PDF is the chapter reference. Printed page ranges appear on each module.
PDF page offsets are irregular; use chapter titles/printed numbers in the book.
All lesson wording, prompts, examples, answer reasoning, and diagrams in the extension are original teaching material.
The scan, book text, and book images are not bundled with the application.

The thirteen chapter families are covered in modules17–29. Module30 checks transfer across them.
The course extends the book with explicit retry boundaries, access checks, failure traces, and operational tests.
A reference is one defensible argument, not a required product list.

Primary references for deeper verification:
- [PostgreSQL row locks and deadlocks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html): reservation/wallet transaction boundaries.
- [Apache Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/): partition logs, consumer positions, and delivery scopes.
- [Stripe idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests): provider-specific key parameters and retention. Other providers differ.
- [Google SRE monitoring](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/): user symptoms, signal choice, and alert noise.
- [Redis sorted sets](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/): ordered score views.
- [PostGIS ST_DWithin](https://postgis.net/docs/ST_DWithin.html): indexed radius candidates and distance semantics.
- [Amazon S3 multipart upload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html): upload lifecycle and completion.
